articleTitle: A visit to the college for electrical engineering at ilmenau, Eastern Germany
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: SOME DECADES AGO IT WAS CUSTOMARY FOR TRAVELLERS from Europe to remote parts of the globe to present papers to learned societies in which they recorded their observations and experiences with the inhabitants of strange countries. Today the opposite takes place. The years of World War II and those preceding and following it have changed the picture and social structure of Europe to such an extent that travels on that continent are now able to offer very much more interest than that previously afforded by sightseeing and social visits. Even more so, journeys across the so-called Iron Curtain are frequently regarded with the interest and awe previously accorded only to explorers' travels. It is to be regretted that the wartime catchword of the Iron Curtain has remained, because it accentuates an administrative separation between the people of various nations between whom there are no natural barriers.

articleTitle: Items of Practical Interest Read before the Institute on Wednesday, 14th December, 1960 High-Current pulse testing
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: THE HIGH-CURRENT PULSE TESTING WHICH WAS undertaken in the high-voltage laboratory of the University of the Witwatersrand was initiated by a request from the Bernard Price Institute for Geophysical Research in connexion with their work on Paleomagnetism. As certain types of rock cool down from the molten state, the temperature passes through a small band after the rock has solidified, called the Curie point, where the direction of the earth's magnetic field is in fact ‘frozen’ into the rock. Below this temperature subsequent changes in the earth's magnetic field do not alter the direction of this magnetism although the magnitude is influenced by the percentage of magnetic material in the rock and the rate of cooling. Most rocks passed through the Curie point many millions of years ago and thus, by measurements of the direction of this thermo-remanent-magnetism relative to the present geographical poles, it is possible to determine where the magnetic poles were situated at that time. Since it has been determined that the mean magnetic poles coincide with the geographic poles if taken over the period of a few thousand years it is possible to determine where the geographic poles were at that time. This study is known as Paleomagnetism.

articleTitle: Automatic synchronising
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: One of the most important operations in the control of power station plant is that of connecting synchronous machines or a.c. networks in parallel. This operation is generally known as “synchronising“, and can usually be carried out only when the phase position, frequency and voltage of the two systems are as nearly identical as possible. If the respective generating systems have identical voltages and frequencies, the difference between their voltages at any given instant will be zero provided that their phase positions coincide exactly, but if the frequency is not exactly the same a resultant voltage — known as the beat voltage — varying cyclically between a maximum and zero will be produced. The frequency of the beat voltage gives a measure of the frequency difference between the two systems, and is commonly expressed as the “beat period” or time between two successive zero values on the curve. The beat period will increase in length the closer the respective frequencies become. When the phase displacement is zero, the beat voltage will be passing through zero at the same instant, provided that the two system voltages have the same amplitude. The ideal condition therefore for the perfect synchronising of two systems, whose respective frequencies are approximately the same, is that the breaker connecting the two systems closes at the exact moment when the beat voltage (and phase displacement) is zero. For a perfect understanding of all the conditions governing synchronising, it is essential to have very clearly in mind the distinction between frequency, phase position and voltage and how these influence the process of synchronising.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: IN 1942 MR W. FENWICK READ A PAPER BEFORE THIS Institute on the field testing of high-voltage bushings. In the paper he described the instruments used for power factor or loss angle testing on the Victoria Falls and Transvaal Power Company's system which is now the Rand and Orange Free State Undertaking of the Electricity Supply Commission. These instruments were a 100-kV Schering Bridge and a 10-kV test set the latter manufactured by the Doble Engineering Corporation of America. The Schering Bridge lacked portability and it was later given on permanent loan to the University of the Witwatersrand. A second Doble set was purchased subsequently and these two sets have been used for many years to test thousands of high-voltage bushings.

abstract: AN ENGINEER'S ACTIONS AND DECISIONS ARE BASED ON TWO sources of knowledge: (i) Practice or experience, which is gained from the knowledge of how a thing has always been done or of an established method sometimes handed down from father to son, more often from master to apprentice and memorized after repeated imitation. abstract: THIS PAPER IS INTENDED TO PROMOTE DISCUSSION on the widest possible aspects of the design of transmission systems for countries other than Great Britain. It is believed that a companion paper for British conditions is also in course of preparation. In order to assemble the many factors involved in a reasonably logical sequence, the various sections of the paper follow, generally, in the same order as the chronological process of analysis, design, engineering, testing and finally proving a high-voltage system. No attempt has been made to deal with the equally important subjects of the specification, testing, construction, inspection and testing of plant, although it will be readily appreciated that modern systems designed for high circuit loadings are made possible only by the use of the best equipment available.
